title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
intro: When one server can't keep up, you have two choices: make it bigger, or add more of them.

slides.heading: The problem
slides.subtitle: One server has limits.
slides.explain: Every server has a fixed amount of CPU, memory and network. As traffic grows, response times climb until requests start timing out.
points: Requests queue up and slow down

slides.heading: Vertical scaling
slides.subtitle: Make the server bigger.
slides.explain: Also called scaling up: move to a machine with more CPU and RAM. It needs no code changes, so it's the quickest first fix.
points: Has a ceiling: machines only get so big
Still a single point of failure

slides.heading: Horizontal scaling
slides.subtitle: Add more servers.
slides.explain: Also called scaling out: run many copies of your app and share traffic between them. This is how large systems keep growing.
points: If one server dies, others keep serving
Needs a load balancer in front

slides.heading: Stateless servers
slides.subtitle: The key to scaling out.
slides.explain: If a server keeps user sessions in its own memory, the next request may hit a different server that knows nothing. Keep servers stateless and store shared state elsewhere.
points: Store sessions in Redis or a database
Any server can handle any request

slides.heading: Which to choose?
slides.subtitle: Usually both, in order.
slides.explain: Most teams scale up first because it's easy, then scale out when they hit limits or need high availability.

scenario.situation: An e-commerce site runs on one large server before a big sale.
scenario.problem: They upgrade to the biggest machine available. Sale traffic still exceeds it, and when it crashes the whole store is offline.
scenario.fix: Run several smaller stateless servers behind a load balancer and add more during the sale. One crash no longer takes the site down.
scenario.takeaway: Scale up for simplicity; scale out for growth and uptime.

cta: Has your app ever outgrown its server?
